The pictured shape is an \(S\)-tetromino, consisting of \(4\) unit squares.

### 1. Maximum possible number of shapes
Since the \(4\times4\) grid contains \(16\) squares and each shape uses \(4\) squares, at most
\[
\frac{16}{4}=4
\]
shapes could be cut out.

We show that \(4\) shapes cannot cover the grid.

Each shape spans at most \(3\) columns and \(2\) rows, or \(2\) columns and \(3\) rows, so it cannot cover two corners of the \(4\times4\) grid. Thus, if four shapes covered the grid, each corner would have to be covered by a different shape.

Consider the upper-left corner:

- If its shape is horizontal, it occupies the first two squares of the top row and the middle two squares of the second row. Any possible shape covering the upper-right corner then overlaps it.
- If its shape is vertical, the upper-right shape must also be vertical; otherwise they overlap. But with both upper corners covered vertically, any shape covering the lower-left corner necessarily overlaps one of them.

Therefore, four shapes cannot fit, so at most \(3\) shapes can be cut out.

### 2. Three shapes are possible
The following arrangement works, where equal letters form one shape and dots are squares not removed:
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
A&B&B&\cdot\\
A&A&B&B\\
\cdot&A&\cdot&C&C\\
\cdot&C&C&\cdot
\end{array}
\]

Thus \(3\) shapes remove \(3\cdot4=12\) squares, leaving
\[
16-12=4.
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
